acquisition.why: Inbound channels such as SEO on a city domain, paid social and Beehiiv's recommendation network are legal. A £300 budget limits ad testing, and organic growth is slow [E].

onboarding.why: Opt-in signup and paid-tier upgrade run fully on the newsletter platform.

delivery.why: Flight alerts can be parsed and rewritten by AI. A human should check deal quality and avoid scraping that breaches Google's terms. A prompt newsletter needs some curation.

billing.why: Paid tiers on Beehiiv or Substack are handled by Stripe.

support.why: Mostly unsubscribe and refund emails, which agents can handle. A community tier would add moderation work.

scores.R_why: A London-airport deals newsletter is cheap and fits the available hours. However, Jack's Flight Club and Going already serve UK flyers. Data sourcing through Google alerts is fragile under their terms [E].
scores.M_why: UK flight deals are dominated by Jack's Flight Club. AI-prompt newsletters are saturated and commoditising fast. Paid conversion is likely around 1-5% [E].
scores.one_line: Highly automatable and cheap to test, but the UK flight-deal niche is crowded. A hyper-local twist such as off-peak family deals from Gatwick or Stansted is needed [E].

acquisition.why: The source relied on word of mouth and in-person contact. UK food traders are mostly sole traders, so cold email or DMs are barred under PECR. Event and market organiser partnerships need human outreach. SEO demand is tiny [E].

onboarding.why: Self-serve setup with QR generation is possible.

support.why: Live-service failures at busy events need a fast response.

scores.R_why: Easy to build, but selling to UK street-food traders needs physical presence at markets. UK SMS costs and low ARPU (about £40 a month) make the economics thin [E].
scores.M_why: Commodity product. Waitwhile, Qminder, Square and Toast features, plus free WhatsApp-based options, already exist.
scores.one_line: Trivial to build but hard to sell legally without legwork, and it competes with bundled POS features. Not a good agent-run fit.

acquisition.why: App store search and content or creator marketing are legal inbound channels. Social apps face a cold-start network problem that needs heavy marketing [E].

delivery.why: The software runs itself, but trust-and-safety moderation for in-person meetups needs human judgement.

support.why: Safety reports, harassment and abuse handling need a human. The Online Safety Act adds duties.

scores.R_why: A network-effect consumer app needs scale and marketing spend far beyond £300 and 6-8 hours a week. The UK Online Safety Act imposes risk-assessment and moderation duties. Safety liability for in-person meetups is high.
scores.M_why: Incumbents include the featured app, plus Couchsurfing, Meetup, Bumble BFF and Facebook groups. Network effects favour the leader.
scores.one_line: An outlier success. A cold-start problem combined with safety and regulatory load makes it a poor fit for a part-time, agent-run UK test.

acquisition.why: YouTube and short-form discovery are inbound channels, though dependent on the platform.

onboarding.why: There are few customers. A partner deal, if used, needs a human negotiation.

delivery.why: Requires on-site filming of a physical business. Only editing can be AI-assisted.

billing.why: AdSense and sponsorships are paid automatically.

support.why: Comment moderation can mostly be done by agents.

scores.R_why: Ricardo would need to film regularly on location. With a toddler and 6-8 hours a week, this is hard. Monetisation takes many months. The source's own guest says ad revenue never beat his service income.
scores.M_why: Saturated creator space. UK ad rates are moderate. Success is a hit-driven lottery.
scores.one_line: Physical filming caps automation, and revenue is slow and uncertain. Unsuitable unless Ricardo already runs a filmable business.

acquisition.why: The n8n creator marketplace, Gumroad, Lemon Squeezy, SEO and YouTube or X content are all inbound. Results depend on the platform.

delivery.why: Agents can build templates with Ricardo reviewing them. Updates are needed when APIs change.

billing.why: Lemon Squeezy or Paddle act as merchant of record and handle UK and EU VAT.

support.why: Buyers ask technical setup questions. Agents can draft answers, but edge cases need Ricardo.

scores.R_why: Fits his technical skills well. A £300 test (domain plus a marketplace listing) can be done in a few weekends. All claims in the source are hypothetical, though.
scores.M_why: Thousands of free n8n templates exist, and AI can generate workflows on demand. Paid templates need a niche, for example UK-specific Xero or HMRC MTD workflows [E].
scores.one_line: Cheap, technical and mostly automatable. AI commoditisation and free alternatives cap prices, so it needs a UK-specific niche angle [E].

acquisition.why: Content and an audience are legal inbound channels. Growth depends on Ricardo's personal brand and credibility, which takes time.

delivery.why: Recorded content runs itself, but calls or events need Ricardo in person.

support.why: Refunds and learner questions. Value usually requires a human presence.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has no established audience or entrepreneurial track record to sell on. Generic business education depends on credibility.
scores.M_why: Massively saturated, and free AI tutors and YouTube substitute for it. The source admits a 3% outcome rate.
scores.one_line: A credibility-led, saturated market where the evidence is promotional. A poor fit for an unknown, agent-run operator.

acquisition.why: SEO, directories, Product Hunt, affiliates and cross-selling are legal inbound channels. The source explicitly avoids cold DMs to individuals.

delivery.why: Web tools and agents, with Ricardo deciding exceptions.

billing.why: Stripe or a merchant of record.

support.why: Maintaining a portfolio adds support load. Agents can triage.

scores.R_why: Technically feasible to start with one tool and £300. The portfolio effect only comes after years, and the source claims 1-3 years of internal use per product. Hours limit how many tools Ricardo can maintain [E].
scores.M_why: A flood of thin AI wrappers in 2026, and foundation-model features absorb them. SEO is volatile because of AI Overviews.
scores.one_line: The most agent-native model here. It works if Ricardo targets one persona he knows and accepts a slow SEO compounding curve; the $3M a year figure is an outlier.

acquisition.why: Virality through sharing loops is legal and inbound but hit-driven. The source had 4M followers. Recruiting guest hosts needs human outreach [E].

onboarding.why: No signup is needed to play.

delivery.why: AI can generate daily questions, with a human fact-check. The game engine runs unattended.

billing.why: Ad network payouts and Stripe Pro subscriptions.

support.why: Minimal. Mostly bug reports and wrong-answer complaints.

scores.R_why: Cheap and fun to build with Ricardo's skills. A UK spin such as Premier League, London Underground or UK history trivia is plausible. Without an audience, a viral launch is unlikely [E]. Ads need a cookie consent management platform.
scores.M_why: Post-Wordle daily-game glut, and games are easily cloned. Programmatic ad rates on low UK traffic are small.
scores.one_line: Low cost and highly automated, but revenue depends on lottery-like virality. The source's success relied on a 4M-follower founder.
